title: Pauli instability in arbitrary states: detecting magic in physical correlators
abstract: Measures of non-stabilizerness (``magic'') of a quantum evolution quantify how hard it is to simulate on a classical computer. A natural question is how to extract information about magic from physical correlators, for example at finite temperature or in the ground state. In this paper we show how to measure magic using out-of-time-order correlators evaluated in an arbitrary state. For every full-rank state, and in particular for every Gibbs state, the resulting quantity vanishes if and only if the evolution is Clifford. We establish its basic properties, relate it to the stabilizer entropy of the Choi state, and prove that, even with a single fixed probe operator, it gives a lower bound on the number of $T$ gates needed to implement the dynamics in any circuit architecture.
summary: This paper introduces a generalized Pauli instability measure, $I_\alpha(ho, U)$, to quantify the 'magic' or non-stabilizerness of quantum dynamics. It proves that this measure vanishes if and only if the evolution is Clifford, providing a rigorous way to detect non-Clifford gates. The measure is shown to yield lower bounds on the number of T gates needed to simulate the dynamics in physical systems.
main_problem: The paper aims to quantify the 'magic' or non-stabilizerness of a quantum evolution, which measures the difficulty of classically simulating the dynamics.
main_result: A generalized Pauli instability measure, $I_\alpha(ho, U)$, was introduced, which is zero if and only if the evolution $U$ is Clifford, and it provides lower bounds on the number of non-Clifford gates (T gates) required for simulation.
method: The authors adapt Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs) to evaluate the instability measure in arbitrary quantum states $ho$, establishing its basic properties and relating it to stabilizer entropy.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on quantum evolution governed by a unitary $U$ acting on a system of $n$ qubits, utilizing Pauli strings ($P_n$) and considering various states like Gibbs or ground states.
key_observables: The generalized Pauli instability measure, $I_\alpha(ho, U)$, and the expectation value of Pauli correlators $	ext{Tr}(ho A(t) B A(t) B)$.
important_parameters: The exponent $\alpha$ (often $\alpha=2$), the state $ho$ (e.g., maximally mixed, Gibbs), and the number of non-Clifford gates ($k$) in the circuit decomposition.
main_assumptions: The faithfulness of the measure requires the state $ho$ to be full-rank; some bounds rely on approximations for error terms in time evolution.
figures_summary: Figures compare the Pauli instability measure $\mathcal{I}_2(ho, U; A)$ over time $t$ for random-matrix dynamics, showing different growth rates for integrable versus non-integrable Hamiltonians.
paper_structure: The paper develops the general measure $I_\alpha$, proves its basic properties (covariance, additivity), establishes its equivalence to the Clifford property, and then applies it to derive quantitative bounds on the T-gate count for various physical models.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, computable diagnostic tool directly linking fundamental quantum information concepts (magic, T-count) to measurable physical correlators in many-body systems.
